query: A Door That Wasn't There {~In a corridor you walk every day there is a door that wasn't there yesterday, small and arched, with a brass handle worn by hands that aren't yours.|A door has appeared in the bare wall by the stairs, painted a cheerful blue, with no keyhole.|There's a new door at the end of a corridor that used to just end. Behind it, something is ticking.} {~The castle does this. It always puts them back.|Nobody else seems to notice it.|It's slightly ajar.} Open it and look inside {~Behind it is a tiny library of books about doors, all open at the same page. You read for an hour, and when you come out, it's gone.|Behind it is a cupboard full of preserved pears, labelled in a hand from two centuries ago. You take one. It's delicious, and the door is gone by supper.|Behind it is a room full of clocks, every one of them right. You set your watch by them and leave, and the door seals behind you.} {~Behind it is a spiral stair up to nowhere. Halfway, the steps get narrower than your foot, and you come down with a turned ankle and the door gone.|Behind it is a broom cupboard, and the brooms are not pleased to see you. You leave with bruises.|Behind it is a room full of clocks, all of them striking at once, right in your ears. You stagger out with a headache that lasts till bedtime.} Chalk a cross on it, walk on {~You chalk a neat cross on it, like the old marks you've seen on other walls. By tomorrow the door is gone, but your cross is still there.|You mark it and keep walking. Some doors are invitations; some are tests. You don't feel like being tested today.|You leave your mark and a note of the date. You're keeping a map of where the doors appear. The castle, you suspect, is keeping one of you.}
